blocks.x: Joseph Clark

My name is Joseph Clark. I was born February 12, 1894. My father's name is Aaron Warren Clark. He was born in 1876. He died September 14, 1894. He was a musician before I was born. And after I was born, before I was born, he'd taken sick. And he told my mother never to let me play a wind instrument. And my mother always kept that pruned into me never to play a wind instrument. And after I began to grow, it just looked like I'd taken a feeling from music. And I was a very small boy. I used to follow bands. And she used to whip me for following bands. And I, um, wait a minute, Mr. Russell.
I wanted to ask you a couple questions. Where was your father born, you said?
My father was born in Louisville, Kentucky. And where did he get his musical train? He got his musical train at Streets University. I see.
Here in New Orleans?
In New Orleans.
He moved here when he was young?
He came here, they came here when he was real young. He went to school here. He was, graduated here. He came here as a small boy. I see.
So you were born right here?
I was born at 2016 Josephine Street.
Uptown?
Mm-hmm.
Where did you go to school?

Well, my first school, my first school was fifth school. That's the old school that used to be at Perdido and Franklin. They call it Liola now. I went there, I went there four times. My mother took me from there and sent me to Straits Junior, which was around the corner from Straits University on the canal. It was around on Tonti. I went there two years. And I left there and I went to Southern.
That was a public school that you went to then? No, a pay school.
Was it a Catholic school?
No, it wasn't a Catholic school. You weren't Catholic?

No, I didn't go to no Catholic school. And I went to Southern. And I went to Southern and I quit school when I was thirteen years old. And I went to work because my mother was going in her evening life. She used to make cigars for a living. And it was so hard on her to try to school me and clothe me and give me what I wanted. And I just quit school and went to work to help her.
How old were you when your father died and now?
I was seven months old when my father died. I was raised without a father.
You never saw him? You never remembered?
No, no more than to see his picture.
What instrument did he play?

He played baritone. He played baritone in the old Onward band. The original Onward, the old Onward, way back in 1880 something. And then he played a while, he used to play with the Pickwood band and also the Excelsior. But after he passed, why different men in that band began to pass and he taken sick and died. Now his last parade was the 10th of May parade. My mother used to tell me that all the time. It was the 10th of May. And he came home and he taken the bed and never got up no more. That was in May and he died that September. What's the meaning of the 10th of May?
Is that a particular day?

Well that's a day that the Oddfellas, that used to be an Oddfellas day here. Years ago when I was a boy, that used to call that Oddfellas day. The 10th of May, regardless to what day it fell on, that was their day. It was Sunday or Monday or any day, that was their day. And they, in the later years, I don't know, they just changed it into the second Sunday in May. They still have it in May, but they changed it to the second Sunday in May. They don't have the 10th of May anymore, unless that Sunday falls on the 10th.
What were the other big days for parades when you were a little boy?

Well, the 30th of May was a big day, but they didn't have parades. They'd have a big encampment down at Chalmette. And people would go down there in the morning with carriages. Automobiles wasn't so plentiful like they are now. People would go down there in carriages. And they would spend their day down there. They'd take baskets and have like pigments. And they would have little ceremonies and they'd have a band of music to play. Just like we do now. But it's not like the old time. Just a few of the old ones come. And when the old ones are gone, there'll be no more Memorial Day not for New Orleans. Because the younger, younger fellas, they're not interested in that. They don't care about that at all. They'll come and listen at the band and they'll stay a while and they'll go. But those people used to stay all day long, up until almost dark.
What kind of music would they have at all?
They'd have brass bands. They'd have brass bands.
Is that right in the Chalmette Cemetery?
That's in the Chalmette Cemetery, down below the city.
Because there's another little settlement there, you know, a colored settlement, a Tronsonville, something like that. They're still celebrated. Yeah.

Yeah, they go. But this is just below. You know where the Chalmette Monument is? Well, just below, just about a quarter of a mile below that, that's the cemetery. You're turning off the highway to the right. That's the cemetery.
I thought maybe it was that little village that celebrated.
No, no, this is on this side of that little village. I know the village you're speaking of. That's on this side of that village.
Because I went to a Memorial Day dance once, they had a few bands down there.
Well, you've been down there when they had a band in the center? No, I've never had a band in the center. Well, his boy had it this year, John.
Well, John, John's...
We just get you.

You see, John, I don't know. You see, they wanted us last year. But we had a job in sight before that particular day. That's why we didn't get it. But I think the union's going to send us there this year.
Well now, what kind of, would they play hymns? Would they play marches?
They would play marches.
Only marches.

You see, when I was a boy, the brass bands of them days, they didn't play this orchestration numbers like these bands play on the street now. That's why we fight so hard to keep the brass bands like they should be. You see, that's like they kid me and tell me that I'll walk ten miles to get a march. In other words, kid me, but I don't walk. I wrote to every house there is to get a certain funeral march and I can't get it. I've asked Mr. Russell. I've asked Mr. Crawford. I've asked this boy Meads in Omaha, Nebraska. And asked him to try to find those two funeral marches for me, but they can't be found. Now I don't know what happened to the plates. Some house has got it and I know it. Somebody, some house has got those plates, but they're just not. It was Cedar Mound and Hazel Grove. It was two beautiful funeral marches. Because the original tuxedo band used to play those marches. I don't mean this tuxedo band of the day. The original tuxedo band. Who was the leader of that band? Papa Celestine.
And when you were a boy you said they didn't play orchestrations? They didn't have? Not on the street.
What did they use?
They used marches.
They used marches.
And they had marches from out of town or did they arrange them themselves?

No, they'd get marches from the houses. Such as Pepper, Barnhouse, Jenkins, and Southwell, and what's this other house now? I can't think of the other house now. Oh, Delby. Jacob. Delby was in, where's his name? I tried, I wrote them, but that house is closed. Oh, it's right across the river from Omaha, Nebraska. It's right on the end of my tongue and I can't close it.
We can find it. We'll look at a map. What is the difference between those brass bands of that day and the ones of today?

Well, I'll tell you. The difference is now, you see, the brass bands of the day, they don't have the instrumentation like the old brass bands. You see, just like our band. We try to get up to it, but we can't. Because nobody, the young fella, don't want to play the baritone. He don't want to play the alto, which we call the peck horn. And he don't want to play the E flat clarinet. When you have the E flat clarinet, the alto, and the baritone, two trombones, the bass, cornet, three cornets, snad bass drum, you have the real, set up for a brass band. But the fellas up today don't want to play the baritone horn and why, I don't know. Sometimes I wish that I had taken baritone.
How many E flat clarinets are there in town now?

Two to my knowings. Who is that? That's Alphonse Pico and John Cashman. There's the only two E flat players that I know of. There may be some more in the union, these youngsters coming along, you know. But I noticed these school bands, I don't see any E flats. I see a lot of B flats. You see twenty or thirty B flats but you don't see no E. The fellas, I don't know, they're afraid of that instrument like they are the oboe. I hear those fellas, those oboe players, they say that the oboe jar is your head. I don't know why. But the mouthpiece look like a cigar holder.
It's different. Yeah it's different. Did they have many oboe players when you were young?
Oh quite a few. Quite a few. I didn't know them but I remember seeing them. Quite a few.
Did they use saxophones in those old bands?
No.
When did they start?

They used clarinet. See they used the clarinet and the alto and the baritone. You see the alto gives you a compliment just like a banjo do in an orchestra. And we call it the peck horn. Because he just makes the same note mostly all the time. Now and then he'll change his note. See what I mean? Yeah I know the part. You see that's the way, that's the set up. But the fellas don't want to play that instrument. Now when I came into the Eureka band we had E flat clarinet, alto and baritone. I was playing trombone then. We had three cornets and two drums. Used to use eleven men. When did you join the Eureka? Well I joined the Eureka about 1934.
You weren't one of the founders then?

No I'm not a founder. But it hadn't been organized very long when I joined. But I remember when it was organized. Because I was playing in a concert band at that time. It says a man here by the name of Henry Pritchett. He set up a concert band of thirty pieces. Still here? Oh he's still here. Yes. But I mean he don't fool with any bands anymore because he's pretty foreign age now.
You still live down there near St. Bernard someplace?
Yeah. Yeah. He lives on 1712 St. Louis. That's near St. Louis Cemetery. Yeah.
Oh we're looking him up. I see.
Yeah he's a tailor. He has a shop on South Ramport there. I think 222 and a half.
I thought he lived way down in Louisville.
No he lived 1712 St. Louis. I mean St. Louis near Claiborne.
He's right next to Johnny's Music. That's right.
Right next door to Johnny's Music. You told me about him he is. That's right.
I forgot to look.
You ought to go down and talk with him.
He's a fine musician.
What was his band called? Tonic Triad. He took that band to Hot Springs, Arkansas in 29 and won every prize there was. Every prize there was we won it.
Oh how often do those old brass bands play by ear? I wanted to get this straight.
Well I'll tell you I really can't answer for that. Because the bands that I used to follow they used to use music.
Did you ever play any hymns?
Well now and then they would play a hymn like if they bring a body out of a house, out of a church, they may play, Near My God To Thee or What a Friend We Have in Jesus.
Did they ever have a fast like By and By or Glory Land?

Well sometimes they would play Glory Land coming up to a house or a church. Fast and slow. No they would play that like we do when we come up to a house or church. You see but when they leave that they'd go in those packs and stay in those packs until they got to the cemetery. They didn't play no head numbers for a funeral.
But they would play head, the hymns would be by head?

Yeah well sometimes. Sometimes. Then they had a book at that time we used to call it, they used to call it a little red book. It had a lot of hymns in it, different hymns, they would use those books. You see? Like Church in the Wild, Wood and all such as that. Lead Kindly Life, they'd use those books. But the bands I don't know, they got away from it, you know, from those books. In other words a lot of them got away from the music. I hate to say it but it's true.
Yes well I wanted to get that straight to the dates on that. When did they start playing pretty ratty in the street?
Oh that's way back, that's way back. Oh that's... When they start playing ratty in the street that's... Oh I guess... I guess back in the 19th century.
Even there when they played all those arrangements on the way to the funeral, on the way to the graveyard, coming back from the graveyard they'd play ratty all the time, even in the old days.

Some would and some wouldn't. Now they're on within the excelsis, they wouldn't do that. Tuxedo, nil. They'd play sometime, you know those organizations ask you to play ratty number for them. You see? They didn't ask for it, those fellows played those marches.
They played the music.

Stars and stripes or whatever they were. Stars and stripes and such as National Emblem, Under Fire, Under Arms, and what's this other march now? Oh we used to play that thing. I can't say... Rifle Rangers, all such as that.
The things like Didn't He Ramble and those...
Well now and then they would play that. Now and then. But they got away from that. I haven't heard a band play that in a long, long time. They got away from that too. That's funny.
It's funny how they come and they go. They're wearing them out.
They come and they go. Now sometimes, sometimes somebody may ask for it. You see.
Well look at Gettysburg, what did you tell me about that? I think you were the one who was telling me how you wore it out.
Oh yeah, we played Gettysburg. That's a good march.
You never play it anymore though, huh?

Well I'll tell you what happened. You see those cards, they got so faded and they turned, they changed colors on us. You see. And then you know those fellas making those stops and they eat their hands, be greasy, you know, and they put their hands on the card and there it is. You see.

Well we could get copies made of those, why we'd like to do that, you know, and keep them on file at Tulane. So you, and seal them up, you know, and if you, if you want to have them refer to them again, you got it. We could do that, you know.
Well let me see. Not give them to anybody else. Now, uh, I think it's Barnhouse. I'm not sure. But there's one of those houses that publishes that. I don't know whether it's Barnhouse or Fillmore.
It publishes which? Gettysburg.
Gettysburg.
But I mean if ever there's a piece, you know, that you can't replace, we'll get copies of it made because you know we'd like to keep a copy. I said we've got a camera specially made. You know.
You see like Gettysburg, like Gettysburg, American Soldier, Panama, those marches are standard. Panama is a standard. They played that when I was a boy.
And it was written, huh?

Yeah it was written but I don't know what happened to it. The fellas got so used to it that they really don't use the music of it anymore. But it was written. By whom I don't know. Do you remember High Society? You ever seen the music for that when you were in high society?
No I never did see the music of High Society.
I wonder if all the parts that you play in Panama are on the music, if they made up new parts
or what? That's very hard to see. It'd be interesting to look into that.
We'll find the music sometime for the marches. Because it is, I think they added a part.
They added a part to Panama?
Yeah they hit a high note and then go down. You know that trumpet part?
I see.
Because a tubo player I know on the west coast told me, he says that's not on the rhythm.

Well I remember when Louis Armstrong was here, he was playing in the Tuxedo Brass Band at that time. And they used to play Panama. And he used to make that high note. And they felt like Louis Armstrong was true, I knew Louis all my life. Practically all my life. See, but I never did play with him. See, I never had the opportunity to play with him because I wasn't just up to it. I was just crawling in the manner of speaking.
What year did you start playing an instrument?
I started about 1921.
About 1921. On trombone?
Trombone, that's my first instrument.
Her mother?

My mother didn't want me to do it but after she saw that I was just headlong to do it, she said, well you're grown now and I can't tell you what to do. But that's your father's wish for you never to play a wind instrument. Why don't you play a string instrument? I told her that I don't like a string instrument.
Which I did too.

After I'd taken it up, I really wanted it. So I talked to my teacher, the man that taught me. And he knew my father. And I asked him about it. He says, well, I'll tell you, in the days that your father started and I started, they didn't make anything but solid brass instruments. They didn't play them like they do now. He says, you don't have to worry about tasting brass. If you would happen to take sick or anything, or inhaling that, drawing your breath from that brass, you'd never feel because that brass, that instrument is coated in and out. You see, in those days all the instruments were brass, solid brass. It wasn't coated like they are now. See, because I can remember way back, there used to be a bass player around here by the name of Pierre, had an upright bass, what they called a monster. It was an E flap but it was a big one. And it had a bell almost as big as a bell of mine. They used to call it the monster E. And it was solid brass. And when he shined that thing you could look at it if he walked in the sun.
And what does tasting that brass do to you?

Well you just taste it all the time when you cough. You know you have a cough and you taste it. Because my mother told me, my father used to tell her, every time he coughed, nor I tasted brass. But things have changed now.
I just wondered if it would have gotten your blood or if it got your tongue off?

No, in some kind of way it gets into your Bronicle II, some kind of way down in there, I don't know. You see, but I was taught never to breathe in an instrument. When you take your breath, I was taught to take my breath from the corner of my mouth. Never take your breath right from the instrument. I always take my breath from the corner of my mouth. I was taught that.
Who was your teacher, Brother Ray? When did you start up?
Oh, Dave Perkins. He's dead, he's been dead now I guess, oh twenty, oh I guess thirty some odd years. Because he died before my mother did.
Did you ever happen to know who he played with, some of the bands he played with? Well no I didn't.

But he used to talk, he used to tell me all the time about my father. He said I knew Aaron well and he was a good baritone player, a wonderful baritone player. He says, and I used to play trombone with him sometime in the Pickwood band. But you see he was mostly, Dave was mostly an orchestra man. He was mostly an orchestra man. In fact he played all the instruments. Bass, trombone, baritone, trumpet, he taught all the instruments and he played all of them. Clarinets, saxophones, axillophones, he taught all the instruments and he played every one of them.
Did you ever see him play drums in any band?
No, I never seen him play any drums. But I've seen him play all the wind instruments. I've seen him play all the wind instruments. I saw him play all the wind instruments.
I saw a picture of him as a drummer one place.
Well he taught Francis to money a drums. You know Francis? I don't think so. He's a friend of Raymond.
He said he was in Papalina, I thought he was playing drums in that band. Well we'll ask Francis. How long did you take lessons?

Well Mr. Russell I'll tell you. I didn't take lessons very long because he passed. I took lessons I guess about a year and ten months. And he'd taken sick. And when he'd taken sick he couldn't teach anymore. Well I was pretty well going then. Because what he put in this I kept it there. And after he passed it just looked like I didn't have confidence in anybody else to teach me. Because he used to tell me all the time the way the fellas used to make you have jitney like that. He didn't teach you that way. He taught you four full time. One, two, three, four.
Moving your foot to the side.

That's right. He taught you waltz this way. That's the way he taught you to beat waltz time. If you would forget and do this he said don't jitney here. He'd call that jitney. He didn't want you to hit your heel on the floor.
You come down on the one beat only.

You come down on the one beat. Waltz time you beat it one, two, three. One, two, three. Four full time is one, two, three, four. One, two, three, four. You always come up on the fourth beat. See? That's the way he taught you four full time.
Remember the method, the book you started in? What kind of a book it was?
Well I started in Artur Langlands. Artur Langlands.
That's right. That's what he used.
That's right. I used Artur Langlands.
After you learned to play then what was your first job? Do you remember your first band you played in?

Well the first band I ever played in, the boys that were taking lessons there, we set up a little brass band just amongst us scholars. And he'd take us one Sunday evening in the yard. He'd sit us in his yard. And that's how we started playing. Every other Sunday we would go and we'd sit in that yard. They had about ten of us.
Did those fellas continue on?
Some did and some didn't. Some did and some didn't. Who were they?
Do you remember any of them?

Well Anderson Minor, we called him Gulley, he was taking bass at that time. And Joe Harris, which is dead, he was taking trombone. And another fella by the name of Jefferson Butler, he was a trumpet player, he's dead. And fella by the name of Henry Williams, he don't play anymore now. He's a minister now. And Felix Goff, clarinet. What did Henry Williams play?
Trumpet.
And Felix Goff, he was on the clarinet and had another boy on the E flat clarinet called Stewart. I don't know what happened to him. He went out of the picture all at once, I don't know.
Is that Joey G. Stewart?

No, his name was Stewart. He had another name now, I just can't, but that was his first name, Stewart. Little short fella. And our drummers was a boy by the name of Jumerville, and another boy by the name of Dito, which Dito is dead now. Jumerville was the bass drummer and Dito was the snare drummer. And we just kept on with that little band like that so funny. We just worked ourselves up in two bands.
You didn't have a name?
No, we didn't name him. You didn't work professionally?
No, no. What do you think about Dave Perkins? Where did he teach? Where did he live?

He lived on 6th between Dryden and Barone. I just forget the number. But that old house is sitting there yet. When I passed there many times, I said, that's the house I was calling, nothing's called the other time then.
That's near Willie Hightower's ice cream parlor.
You remember Willie Hightower, the trumpet player, the carnet?
Yeah, I remember him. In the ice cream parlor?
I remember him.
I remember him.
He tells about Dave Perkins walking by his place.
Yeah.
He used to take his walk every evening, every night rather, after he'd get through teaching. And if it was 10 or 10.30 he'd take his walk every night. Every night he'd take his walk.
Did he have many students? Oh yeah.
He had a lot of students. He had a lot of students. White and colored.
Somebody said something about him renting horns. Did he have a lot of horns on the other?
He did. He did. He had trombones, trumpets, drums, and banjos and all that kind of stuff. Up in his loft he had all that stuff up there.
Where'd you get your first trombone?

My first trombone? I bought that trombone from a man that used to play in the Shrine Band. And he told me, Dave was teaching me at that time, and I told him I wanted to buy one so I could have it to practice at home. And he saw this man that played in the Shrine Band and he bought it from me. And I only paid $40 for it. And I kept that trombone, oh I guess about eight years or nine years. Then I was looking in a catalog one day from H.N. White. They built a King instrument. And I saw a trombone in there that I liked. And I ordered that trombone and it had a five and a half inch bell.
That's a small one.

Small bell, yeah. And I ordered that horn. That horn cost me $225 at that time. And I kept that horn until I went on the bass. But I was forced on the bass overnight. Yeah, we had a funeral for the Young Men Olympia. And Dominic Raimi was leading the band at that time, which we called him T-Boy. And we had hired Professor Dalmas, I guess you know him.
No I don't.

You heard of him though, yeah? Well we hired him to play bass. But he didn't have a bass so we got the bass from our bass player which was sick Pete Blanchett. So we brought the bass over to the hall and we waited for him and he didn't come. And it was time to leave. So T-Boy said to me, he says, go in the hall and get that bass. I says, I can't play no bass man. Go get the bass like I'm telling you. Well I went and got the bass but I had never played bass before. I've had them in my hands but I never even tried to play them.
You see?

I could feel the horn all right. So she just go ahead. Said that'll make the band, the band won't look short. Even if you can't play the bass the band would have looked for them. So we made that funeral. So when we got in he says to me, he says, you take that bass home. I'm going to Pete and tell Pete that you got that bass and I'm responsible for it. You go to World Airlines and you buy your chart. Just for the finger, not the music. You know the music. The music is the same. And I went to World Airlines and bought a chart the next day. And I came on home. So my wife says, well, what you going to do now? I says, well I'm going to try to play this bass. And I sit there with that bass and I just kept on. And I've never taken a lesson from nobody, not on the bass. No more than that chart I learnt the finger. To take a lesson on the bass I got to take that chance. So dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear

segments.title: Birth, father Aaron Clark, and the warning against wind instruments
segments.summary: Clark gives his birth date and says his father, a musician, died months after he was born and told his mother never to let him play a wind instrument. He followed bands as a child anyway. Interviewers ask where his parents came from and where he was born.

segments.title: Schools and leaving school at thirteen to work
segments.summary: Clark names the schools he attended and quit at thirteen to help his mother, a cigar maker. He never knew his father.

segments.title: His father in the Onward, Pickwood and Excelsior bands
segments.summary: His father played baritone in the old Onward, Pickwood and Excelsior bands. His last parade was the 10th of May Oddfellows day.

segments.title: Memorial Day at Chalmette and Clark's current band work
segments.summary: Clark describes the big May 30th encampment at Chalmette cemetery with brass bands, which the younger generation no longer cares about. Talk turns to whether his band is booked there.

segments.title: Marches versus orchestrations and the lost funeral marches
segments.summary: Brass bands of his boyhood played marches and not orchestrations. Clark has been unable to find two funeral marches the original Tuxedo band played, and names the publishing houses.

segments.title: Brass band instrumentation and the missing E flat clarinets
segments.summary: Clark describes the proper brass band set-up of E flat clarinet, alto, baritone, trombones, cornets and drums. Few young players take up baritone or E flat clarinet.

segments.title: No saxophones in old bands; joining the Eureka band around 1934
segments.summary: Old bands used clarinet, alto and baritone, not saxophones. Clark joined the Eureka band about 1934, playing trombone, in an eleven-man line-up.

segments.title: Henry Pritchett and his Tonic Triad band
segments.summary: Clark recalls Henry Pritchett, who organised a thirty-piece concert band, and gives his address and tailor shop. His Tonic Triad band won every prize at Hot Springs in 1929.

segments.title: Hymns, marches and what brass bands played for funerals
segments.summary: Clark describes the old bands reading music, playing hymns from a little red book, and playing marches on the way back from the cemetery. Didn't He Ramble was played only occasionally.

segments.title: Gettysburg, Panama and preserving worn band music
segments.summary: Clark explains that the Gettysburg parts faded and became greasy. The interviewers offer to copy his music for Tulane. They discuss Panama and its added high trumpet part.

segments.title: Louis Armstrong in the Tuxedo Brass Band
segments.summary: Clark recalls Louis Armstrong playing Panama in the Tuxedo Brass Band and says he knew him all his life but never played with him.

segments.title: Starting trombone in 1921 despite his father's wish, and the fear of tasting brass
segments.summary: Clark began trombone about 1921, over his mother's objection. His teacher said solid-brass instruments were never harmful, and Clark was taught to breathe from the corner of his mouth.

segments.title: Teacher Dave Perkins and his versatility
segments.summary: Dave Perkins knew Clark's father and taught and played all instruments. The interviewers ask whether he also played drums.

segments.title: Length of lessons, beating time, and the Langley method book
segments.summary: Clark studied with Perkins for about a year and ten months until Perkins fell sick. Perkins taught four-four and waltz time by foot, and Clark started on the Langley method.

segments.title: First band: the pupils' yard band
segments.summary: The first band was a group of Perkins's pupils who played in his yard on Sundays. Clark lists the members.

segments.title: Dave Perkins's home, evening walks and many students
segments.summary: Clark describes where Perkins lived, his nightly walk past Willie Hightower's ice cream parlor, and his many white and colored students.

segments.title: Clark's first trombone and the King trombone he ordered
segments.summary: Clark bought his first trombone for $40 from a Shrine Band player. After about eight years he ordered a King trombone with a five and a half inch bell for $225.

segments.title: Forced onto bass at a Young Men Olympia funeral
segments.summary: At a Young Men Olympia funeral with Dominic Remy leading, the hired bass player did not show up, and Clark was made to play the bass. He bought a fingering chart and taught himself.
